title: Agent factory
tagline: A repo-agnostic system where agents write, test and review every pull request, and a human decides only what needs judgment.
why: Of the last 100 merged pull requests in the pipeline repo (first-party count of public PR history, 5 November 2026), 46 came from an external autonomous builder whose trial ended on 6 November, and every review on record came from a single account. The do-nothing baseline is review that runs through one person's attention, so throughput is capped by it.
mission: A portable gate any repo can adopt. By design, tests will run PR code with no credentials, a reviewer agent will see only the diff, as data, with no tools, and each change will be sorted into a risk tier. Low-risk tiers will merge without a human; privacy code, migrations and workflow files will always stop for a person.
destination: Phase 0 (target 13 November) ends with a pilot on the pipeline repo: a change that touches only documentation merges with no human touch, and a change to a protected area such as privacy code or workflow files stops for a person. After that, the reviewer is back-tested on past pull requests with known defects, and a day-14 read-out against the baseline decides whether it stays.
showcase: Designing trust boundaries for agents: by design, untrusted text, private data and write access will never meet in one job
Designing the gate to fail closed: a missing or malformed verdict, an expired token or a usage limit will block the merge instead of passing it
Red-teaming a design before building it, and treating its blockers as entry criteria rather than backlog
Risk tiering by design, where any file path the rules don't recognise falls into the strictest tier
Holding an agent system to a do-nothing baseline and a day-14 kill rule, so quality per token decides whether it stays

milestones.note: Built in its own public repository and through three review rounds (first-party, 7 November 2026). It has run only in local tests so far.

milestones.title: Separate identities for authoring, approving and merging

decisions.decision: Split identities: an agent account authors, an app approves low-risk tiers, and a person approves guarded paths in the browser.
decisions.why: Authoring, approving and merging should be distinct roles that can be audited separately.

decisions.decision: Run agent code review on every code PR, with no rubric or score, and a kill rule at day 14.
decisions.why: A reviewer that runs on every change has to prove it's worth its cost, so the test is quality per token.

decisions.decision: Keep the gate's core in its own public repository, so each project adopts it by pinning a version.
decisions.why: A repo-agnostic system needs one home and one version history, not a copy per project.

open.question: After the pilot, back-test a reviewer from a second model provider against the in-house reviewer, and keep it only if it catches real defects the first one misses?

risks.risk: Prompt injection: a diff can carry text written to talk the reviewer into approving.
risks.mitigation: By design, the reviewer will get a stripped diff only, no tools and no PR text, and will need a positive verdict to pass.

risks.risk: The gate has run only in local tests; its behaviour on GitHub is unproven until the live trials.
risks.mitigation: One trial PR per risk tier with auto-merge off, before anything merges on its own.

risks.risk: A reviewer on every PR can spend tokens without catching defects.
risks.mitigation: The day-14 read-out compares cost and catches with the baseline, and the kill rule removes it if it doesn't pay.

log.text: Portable core opened for review in its own public repository, after three review rounds whose findings were closed in its commits.
Go decision taken on all three design questions. Phase 0 build started.
The design went through independent analyses and a red-team pass. Its blockers became entry criteria for the build.
